title: Rivals and Allies
objectives: I can use ten words to talk about conflict, alliances, and surrender.
I can read a history passage and name the events in order.
I can tell the difference between retreat, surrender, and defeat.
I can write about groups that work together or fight.
rationale: Conflict words appear in history and fiction, and students often use fight or win for every kind of struggle. The ten words give precise names for partners (alliance, ally, pact), types of conflict (feud, clash, invade), and ways a conflict can end or stall (retreat, surrender, defeat, stalemate). The passage on the American Revolution puts these words in a true sequence of events. The unit builds on rebel, defy, and injustice from unit 7.

words.def: An agreement between groups or countries to help one another.
words.ex: The two small kingdoms formed an alliance to protect their shared border.
words.ex2: The soccer clubs joined in an alliance to share one practice field.
words.nonExample: Two countries that refuse to speak to each other do not have an alliance.

apps.academic: Historians study how an alliance changed the balance of power in a war.
apps.spoken: Our two classes made an alliance to clean the garden together.
apps.writing: Use alliance for a formal partnership, not for a casual friendship.

words.nonExample: Two friends who agree on every point do not clash.

words.def: A person, group, or country that joins you to help reach a goal.
words.ex: France was an important ally of the American colonies during the Revolution.
words.ex2: My best ally in the science fair was my lab partner, who shared every task.
words.nonExample: A rival who works against you is not an ally.

apps.academic: A country can ask a trusted ally for help when it is attacked.
apps.spoken: I need an ally to help me convince our teacher.
apps.writing: Use ally for someone who supports you in a shared goal or fight.

cloze.s: In the war, the small nation was glad to have a powerful ___ nearby.

cloze2.s: When no one else agreed with Tara, her friend Zane was her only ___ at the meeting.

misuse.s: My ally tried to ruin my project and told everyone my plan.
misuse.why: An ally helps you reach a goal; someone who ruins your project is not an ally.

words.def: A serious agreement between people or groups.
words.ex: The leaders signed a pact never to attack one another.
words.ex2: The twins made a pact to never tell each other's secrets.
words.nonExample: A guess about what might happen is not a pact.

apps.academic: In history, a peace pact can end a war and set new rules for trade.
apps.spoken: We made a pact to study together every Thursday.
apps.writing: Use pact for a serious promise that people make together.

cloze.s: The villages shook hands on a ___ to share their well during dry summers.

cloze2.s: My cousins made a ___ to read one book each week and trade summaries.

misuse.s: They signed a pact, which meant they refused to agree to anything.
misuse.why: A pact is an agreement; refusing to agree to anything is the opposite.

words.def: To enter a place by force to take it over.
words.ex: The army invaded the island at night, hoping to surprise the guards.
words.ex2: Ants invaded our picnic and swarmed over the sandwiches.
words.nonExample: A guest who is invited to a house does not invade it.

apps.academic: The history book explains why one empire chose to invade its neighbor.
apps.spoken: Weeds invade the garden if no one pulls them out.
apps.writing: Use invade for forceful entry that no one invited.

misuse.s: The visiting team invaded our school by waiting politely at the door until they were invited in.
misuse.why: To invade is to enter by force; waiting politely to be invited is not invading.

words.def: To move back or away from danger or a fight.
words.ex: The soldiers retreated up the hill when the enemy reinforcements arrived.
words.ex2: When the dog growled, the little boy retreated behind his mother.
words.nonExample: Marching forward into the fight is not retreating.

apps.academic: The map shows the route where the army retreated after losing the battle.
apps.spoken: I had to retreat indoors when the rain started.
apps.writing: Use retreat for stepping back to stay safe, not for giving up forever.

cloze.s: Seeing the huge wave, the beachgoers had to ___ to higher ground.

cloze2.s: The army chose to ___ across the river rather than fight a stronger enemy.

misuse.s: The brave soldiers retreated by charging forward toward the enemy.
misuse.why: Retreat means moving back; charging forward is the opposite.

words.def: To give up and stop fighting because you cannot win.
words.ex: The tired soldiers surrendered after three days without food.
words.ex2: After a long chess match, Lena surrendered and tipped over her king.
words.nonExample: A team that keeps fighting to the final second has not surrendered.

apps.academic: The history report explains when and why the general chose to surrender.
apps.spoken: I will not surrender my seat on the bus to a loud group of kids.
apps.writing: Use surrender for a clear choice to stop fighting.

cloze.s: Outnumbered and out of supplies, the fort's defenders had no choice but to ___.

cloze2.s: Hoping to score one more point, the player refused to ___ even when far behind.

misuse.s: The army surrendered by attacking again and again with all its strength.
misuse.why: To surrender is to give up; attacking again and again is the opposite.

words.def: To win against someone in a fight or contest.
words.ex: The home team defeated the visitors by two goals.
words.ex2: Marie hoped to defeat her older brother at checkers.
words.nonExample: A tie game means neither team has defeated the other.

cloze2.s: With a clever plan, the smaller army was able to ___ a much larger one.

misuse.why: To defeat someone is to beat them; losing by ten points is the opposite.

words.def: A standoff in which neither side can win or move forward.
words.ex: The talks ended in a stalemate when neither side would change its offer.
words.ex2: The chess game ended in a stalemate, so neither player won.
words.nonExample: When one team scores and wins, the game has not reached a stalemate.

apps.academic: Historians call a war a stalemate when neither army can win a clear victory.
apps.spoken: The argument was a stalemate, since both of us refused to change our minds.
apps.writing: Use stalemate when no one is winning and no one will give in.

cloze.s: The debate reached a ___ because neither team would give up even one point.

cloze2.s: After hours of tugging, the rope stayed still, a ___ between two strong teams.

misuse.s: A stalemate means one side wins quickly and the other side agrees.
misuse.why: A stalemate is a standoff with no winner; one side winning quickly is not a stalemate.

passage.title: Friends Across the Ocean
paras: When the American Revolution began in 1775, the colonies faced a powerful rival. British soldiers and colonial fighters clashed at Lexington and Concord, and the war was on.

The first years were hard. In 1776, a large British army invaded the area around New York. General George Washington's troops were outnumbered, so he ordered them to retreat across the East River at night. The Americans escaped, but the war was far from won.

A year later, in October, Americans defeated a British army at Saratoga, New York. The victory showed France that the colonists could succeed. In February 1778, France signed a pact with the United States, a formal alliance that made France a powerful ally. French ships, soldiers, and money soon arrived.
Even so, progress was slow. For a time in the North, neither side could win, and the war became a stalemate. In many towns, neighbors who disagreed about the war began bitter feuds.

The turning point came in 1781. American and French troops trapped a British army at Yorktown, Virginia. After weeks of fighting, the army had no hope of escape and chose to surrender in October. The war did not officially end until 1783, but the alliance had helped the new nation win.

qs.why: Washington's troops were outnumbered, and they escaped across the river, so retreat means to pull back.

qs.q: Why did the victory at Saratoga matter to France?
choices: It made France afraid of the colonists.
It ended the war right away.
It showed that the colonists had a real chance to win.
It gave France a new colony.
qs.why: The text says the victory showed France that the colonists could succeed, which led to the pact.

qs.q: Which detail best shows how the alliance helped the Americans?
choices: The war began at Lexington and Concord.
French ships, soldiers, and money soon arrived.
Washington's troops retreated across the river.
qs.why: Ships, soldiers, and money are direct help that the ally provided.

qs.q: What does it mean that the war in the North was a stalemate?
choices: The soldiers went home for the winter.
Neither side could win a clear victory.
qs.why: The sentence before the word says neither side could win.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Help from an ally, France, helped the colonists win after hard early years.
British soldiers were stronger than American soldiers.
Neighbors should never disagree about politics.
qs.why: The passage moves from hard early years to the French alliance and the victory at Yorktown.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for conflict and cooperation, read a short history passage about the American Revolution, and write about groups that fight, join, retreat, or give in. The unit builds precise verbs for history and fiction.

notes.va.alliance.n: Alliance is a formal partnership. Ask students how it differs from a friendship, and note that an alliance can end when the shared goal is over.
notes.va.feud.n: Feud is long-lasting and often between families or neighbors. Contrast it with a one-day argument. Ask for fictional feuds students know.
notes.va.clash.v: Clash has two common senses: a fight and colors that do not go together. Teach the fight sense and show the color sense on the card.
notes.va.ally.n: Ally is a noun in this unit; the verb has a different stress. The word ally can also be used for a person in everyday life, not only for countries.
notes.va.pact.n: Pact is short and strong: a serious promise. Point out that pact and treaty overlap, but pact can also be between two friends.
notes.va.invade.v: Invade needs force and no invitation. Contrast with visit. Use an animal or weeds example for the figurative meaning.
notes.va.retreat.v: Retreat is not always a failure. Ask students when stepping back is smart.
notes.va.surrender.v: Surrender is a choice to stop, usually because winning is impossible. Contrast with retreat: a retreating army can still fight later.
notes.va.defeat.v: Defeat is a verb in this unit and needs an object: defeat the champions. Students often say defeat when they mean lost, so model both.
notes.va.stalemate.n: Stalemate comes from chess, where the game ends with no winner when a player has no legal move. Use the chess example and then the debate example.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says the colonists had a pact with France. A pact is a serious agreement, so France is now an ally. I can tell from the word alliance that the two countries agreed to help each other.'
